Embryonated eggs of Crassostrea corteziensis hatch after roughly 5.5 days [ab = roughly 5.5 days] when incubated at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], a duration that mirrors the rapid early development reported for the congeneric Pacific oyster Crassostrea gigas. Upon eclosion, the newly released veliger larvae possess a prodissoconch shell measuring approximately 0.01 cm [Lb = approximately 0.01 cm] in length, a value consistent across both species and indicative of the small energy reserves packaged within the yolk-laden egg. The larval phase proceeds through a succession of free-swimming, planktotrophic stages, during which the developing oyster feeds on phytoplankton and grows steadily. A critical milestone in the larval period is the attainment of metamorphic competence, after which the pediveliger seeks a suitable substrate for settlement. This entire planktonic interval from hatching to settlement, encompassing the feeding and growth phase necessary for the larva to reach the size required for metamorphosis, has been documented to last 14.5 days after hatching  under the same thermal regime, by which point the settling pediveliger has attained a shell length at metamorphosis of approximately 0.034 cm  at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The remarkable similarity in larval growth trajectories between C. corteziensis and C. gigas suggests a conserved developmental program within this genus, governed largely by temperature and the availability of suitable phytoplankton prey.

Following metamorphosis, the newly settled spat of Crassostrea corteziensis enters a phase of rapid somatic expansion. The post-larval transformation involves a complete reorganisation of the body plan, including the loss of the velum and the development of functional gills, enabling the juvenile to adopt a fully benthic, filter-feeding existence. This relatively short interval to puberty reflects a life-history strategy focused on early reproductive output, a trait shared with many other opportunistic bivalve species that inhabit dynamic coastal environments. The rapid transition from a minuscule 0.01 cm [Lb = 0.01 cm] larval shell at birth to a sexually mature juvenile of over 2 cm demonstrates a powerful capacity for tissue accretion driven by the efficient exploitation of suspended particulate organic matter in estuarine and lagoon systems.

For reproductively active adults of Crassostrea corteziensis, the total shell length eventually attained by the oldest and largest individuals in a population, representing the ultimate size ceiling for the species, has been recorded at 13 cm [Li = 13 cm]. At this terminal size, the corresponding soft-tissue dry weight, which excludes the mass of the calcium carbonate shell, reaches a value of approximately 9 grams . This estimate of maximum dry tissue mass, derived from allometric scaling relationships applied to congeneric species, underscores the substantial investment in somatic tissue that supports gamete production. The reproductive biology of this oyster is characterised by a high fecundity typical of broadcast-spawning bivalves. Under the prevailing thermal conditions of their native habitat, which can average 7.8 °C [T = 7.8 °C] in deeper or more temperate portions of their range, the maximum recorded daily reproductive output for a single individual has been estimated to reach 400,000 eggs per day [Ri = 400,000 eggs per day], a prodigious number that ensures at least some larvae will encounter favorable settlement substrates despite the high mortality inherent in planktonic dispersal.

Throughout this lengthy adult phase, individuals continue to add shell material, gradually approaching the asymptotic length of 13 cm [Li = 13 cm], although growth rate slows considerably after sexual maturity as resources are increasingly partitioned towards gametogenesis and the annual spawning cycle.

Comparative studies between Crassostrea corteziensis and its congener Crassostrea gigas have revealed that the timing of early life history events is strikingly congruent under identical thermal conditions. These interspecific contrasts in size and timing highlight the adaptive differentiation that has occurred among eastern Pacific oyster lineages in response to regional environmental regimes, particularly temperature and productivity gradients.
